extracted.intended_audience: general readers, writers and playwrights interested in comedy, satire, and conversational humour
extracted.subtask_short: writing comic essays and stage comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and critical rules about producing comic effect in conversation and on the stage: what makes people laugh, the proper role of a comic 'butt', when bawdiness is a cheap device, and how to use character and virtue to amuse and reform an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause of laughter: oddness or infirmity
rubrics_metrics.description: When a Man of Wit makes us laugh, it is by betraying some Oddness or Infirmity in his own Character, or in the Representation which he makes of others; and when we laugh at a Brute or even an inanimate thing, it is at some Action or Incident that bears a remote Analogy to any Blunder or Absurdity in reasonable Creatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter arises from perceived shortcomings or blunders (in character or action). The essay links the comic effect to a subject falling short of the spectator in specific respects that stir up mirth. Use analogies to human absurdity when attributing comic worth to animals/things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for a conversational 'Butt'
rubrics_metrics.description: A Man is not qualified for a Butt who has not a good deal of Wit and Vivacity, even in the ridiculous side of his Character; a stupid Butt is only fit for the Conversation of ordinary People.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful butt must supply 'play' to clever companions by actively bestowing material for raillery; paradoxically, a witty butt can turn ridicule back on the attacker. Examples: Sir John Falstaff as an accomplished butt. Anti‑pattern: a merely stupid target fails to amuse sophisticated company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flattery by attentive listening as a social/comic device
rubrics_metrics.description: When you fall into a Man's Conversation, the first thing you should consider is whether he has a greater Inclination to hear you, or that you should hear him. The skilful Attention to whatever is uttered is a form of flattery used by able flatterers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For social humour and influence, portray characters who gain favor by listening and reflecting others' thoughts; attention can be comic (or socially effective) when it exposes vanity or dependency in the person being flattered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheap comic expedients: bawdy language, lascivious gesture, double entendres
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Author cannot strike out of himself any more of that which he has superior to those who make up the Bulk of his Audience, his natural Recourse is to Luscious Expressions. It lifts a heavy empty Sentence when there is added to it a lascivious Gesture of Body; and when it is too low to be raised even by that, a flat Meaning is enlivened by making it a double one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are identified as anti‑patterns: recourse for dull writers who lack invention. Use sparingly or avoid; they pander to base appetites rather than elevate taste. Examples: stripping scenes, repeated sexual signals in plays; authors who rely on these are criticised as lacking genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic propriety regarding chastity and modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Such an Image as this ought, by no means, to be presented to a Chaste and Regular Audience. The conduct of the Stage at present with Relation to Chastity and Modesty requires consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights should consider audience sensibilities; explicit sexual images or lines can alienate modest audiences and cause some patrons (notably women) to avoid the playhouse. Revision (trimming lascivious lines) is an appropriate corrective (example: Steele's own retrenchment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer character and moral example to mere titillation
rubrics_metrics.description: If Men of Wit... would turn their Thoughts upon raising it from good natural Impulses as are in the Audience, but are choked up by Vice and Luxury, they would not only please, but befriend us at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create comic works that appeal to 'good natural Impulses' and present virtuous characters, or at least hold vices up to contempt rather than reward them. A proposed dramatic device: instead of rewarding the rakish hero, expose him as a traitor and make him meet with contempt—this both amuses and morally instructs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal comic hero: combine virtue with wit
rubrics_metrics.description: A Man that is Temperate, Generous, Valiant, Chaste, Faithful and Honest, may, at the same time, have Wit, Humour, Mirth, Good-breeding, and Gallantry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design comic protagonists who embody noble virtues alongside wit; such characters can both entertain and reform the audience's tastes. This is presented as a positive model and corrective to plays that reward vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical perspective: avoid provincial contempt for foreign customs
rubrics_metrics.description: We are all guilty in some Measure of the same narrow way of Thinking, when we fancy the Customs, Dress, and Manners of other Countries are ridiculous and extravagant, if they do not resemble those of our own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using travel or ethnographic material for comedy, avoid mere ridicule of difference. Use such perspectives to reveal narrowness in the satirist and to produce more thoughtful, humane humour (example: the mock-Indian journal that misinterprets English customs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Signal vanity and invite satire through costume and affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the young Fellows at the coffee-houses, superiority proceeds from an Opinion of Gallantry and Fashion: the Gentleman in the Strawberry Sash... has subscribed to every Opera... and is supposed to receive Favours from one of the Actresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clothing, affectation, and ostentatious habits as reliable markers of vanity and pretension in comic characterisation. Such external details both amuse and furnish targets for satirical observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage depiction should be mindful of plausibility and social role
rubrics_metrics.description: The difficulty of keeping up a sprightly Dialogue for five Acts together ... authors resort to smuttiness when wit fails. When actors make an Exit on a particular occasion, the Ladies are sure to have an examining Glance from the Pit...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid implausible or repetitive devices (e.g., repeating the same bawdy errand each act) that strain credibility. Aim for credible motivations and variety in action; reliance on stage gimmicks to cover weak dialogue is criticized.
